title: The Fire That Isn't Alive
principle: Getting energy out in small steps, on purpose, is called metabolism.

t: A fire eats, breathes, grows, gives off waste, and makes more fires. It is not alive.

A candle flame takes in fuel and oxygen, gives off carbon dioxide and water, grows, moves, responds to being disturbed, and starts new flames. It fails almost nothing on the list — and it is not alive.
sub: This is the sharpest test the seven signs face, and working out what is absent is the point of the lesson.

question: What has a fire got that a living thing has not?
What does a flame lack that a cell has?
options: Instructions — a fire has no recipe for itself
Fire is too hot to be alive
stages.outcome: Instructions — a fire has no recipe for itself
note: Commit. Two of these are serious answers and one is a red herring about temperature.

stages.label: Compare them
captions: Both use oxygen and give off carbon dioxide. Tie.
Both grow and both spread. Tie.
A cell releases its energy in small controlled steps. A fire lets it all go at once, as heat.
A cell carries instructions for rebuilding itself. A fire carries nothing at all.
t: Go through it point by point and find where they stop matching.
Compare the two systems criterion by criterion. The first three are genuine ties; the last two are not.
after: Controlled steps, and a recipe. Those are the two differences that matter.
Two real differences: energy released in small captured steps rather than all at once, and a heritable specification of the system itself. Everything else was a draw.

t: Getting energy out in small steps, on purpose, is called metabolism.
Releasing energy in small controlled steps and capturing it is metabolism — not simply burning.
Metabolism is coupled, enzyme-catalysed oxidation: the same overall reaction as combustion, run in many small steps so the energy can be captured rather than lost as heat.

Glucose oxidation in a cell and in a flame have identical reactants, products and free energy change. The difference is entirely in the path — roughly thirty enzymatic steps that capture about a third of the available energy in ATP, against one step that captures none.
sub: And a recipe for making another one of you.
Plus heredity: a specification that gets copied. A fire lights another fire but passes on nothing.
Combustion is inheritance-free. A new flame carries no information from the old one, so nothing can accumulate and nothing can improve.

This is why fire is the sharpest counter-example available. It has metabolism-like behaviour with no coupling and reproduction-like behaviour with no heredity — and it isolates exactly the two properties that matter.

q: Why is a fire not alive?
What does a flame fundamentally lack?
Which two properties does combustion lack?
options: It carries no instructions and captures no energy
It is not made of cells
It cannot move on its own
why: A fire does lots of things living things do. But it has no recipe for itself, and it throws all its energy away as heat instead of using it.
No heredity and no coupling. A new flame inherits nothing from the old one, so nothing can accumulate; and the energy leaves as heat rather than being captured to do work.

Both are needed and neither is present. Without energy capture there is nothing to power maintenance; without heredity there is nothing to select on, so a fire cannot adapt in any generation, however many flames it lights.

q: Cells and fires run the same reaction on sugar. So what differs?
Glucose oxidation has the same ΔG in a cell and in a flame. What differs?
options: The path — many small captured steps instead of one uncontrolled one
why: The same sugar and the same oxygen make the same carbon dioxide and water, and release the same amount of energy. A cell just takes it out in about thirty small steps and catches most of it on the way.

Reactants, products and free energy change are identical; only the path differs. Thermodynamics fixes the endpoints and says nothing about the route, which is precisely the freedom enzymes exploit — they cannot change what is possible, only how fast and in what steps, and the steps are where the energy gets captured.

t: Your body runs at about the same temperature all day, even though it is burning fuel constantly.

You dissipate roughly a hundred watts continuously and hold your core temperature within a degree. That is only possible because the oxidation is staged: if a cell released glucose's energy the way a flame does, it would cook itself. Stepwise release is not an efficiency detail — it is what makes the whole arrangement survivable.
